chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from Ali ibn Asbat who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Ridha (peace be upon him) about capability (istita'a). So he said: 'The servant is capable after four characteristics — that he be free in his path, healthy of body, sound of limbs, and there be a cause coming from God.'

He said: I said, 'May I be your sacrifice — explain this to me.' He said: 'If the servant happens to be free in his path, healthy of body, sound of limbs, and he wants to commit adultery but does not find a woman, then he finds her — so either he restrains himself and refrains, just as Yusuf (peace be upon him) refrained, or he yields between himself and his desire and commits adultery, and so is called an adulterer; and he did not obey God by coercion, nor did he disobey Him by being overcome.'

key_terms.الاستطاعة: Istita'a — capability, the theological term for the capacity for moral action and free will
key_terms.سَبَبٌ وَارِدٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ: A cause coming from God — the divinely-provided opportunity or means
key_terms.مُخَلَّى السَّرْبِ: Free in one's path — unobstructed, a condition of being unimpeded

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Ridha say about free will and capability (istita'a) in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ridha (AS) defines the theological concept of istita'a (capability or free will) in response to a direct question. He establishes four preconditions for moral agency — freedom of movement, bodily health, intact limbs, and a divinely-ordained opportunity — and then illustrates the concept with the example of Prophet Yusuf (AS), who exercised free will to resist temptation. This hadith addresses a major Shia theological position affirming human free will against both the Jabriyya (determinism) and Qadariyya (radical free will) extremes, teaching that humans act freely within God-given conditions, neither compelled to obey nor overcome into sin.
